content.intro: In this lesson, you will study search Algorithms in AI within Traditional AI, Logic, Search, and Reasoning. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Traditional AI represents states, facts, goals, and actions explicitly. A search or rule-based method is only as useful as its representation and assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Search explores a state space from an initial state toward a goal. Different strategies trade memory, path cost, completeness, and speed; choose one based on whether edge costs and solution quality matter.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: State spaces and search trees
items.text: Memory or state records information used across workflow steps. Define scope, expiry, reset behavior, access control, and how stale or conflicting information is handled.

items.title: Initial states and goal states
items.text: Memory or state records information used across workflow steps. Define scope, expiry, reset behavior, access control, and how stale or conflicting information is handled.

items.title: Breadth-first search
items.text: Breadth-first search explores states level by level. With equal step costs it finds a path with the fewest edges, but its frontier can use substantial memory.

items.title: Depth-first search
items.text: Depth-first search follows one branch before backtracking. It can use less frontier memory, but without appropriate safeguards it may explore a deep path before a better solution.

items.title: Uniform-cost search
items.text: Uniform-cost search expands the currently cheapest known path. Under standard nonnegative edge-cost assumptions it finds a least-cost path, though it may explore many states.
